title: Wayfinding: A simple concept, a complex process
authors: Anna Charisse Farr, Tristan Kleinschmidt, Prasad Yarlagadda & Kerrie Mengersen, 2012
review_question: To examine the motivations for investigating wayfinding, discuss associated principles and factors from different research perspectives, and review approaches to modelling wayfinding, in order to understand this seemingly simple but complex process.
inclusion_exclusion_criteria: Not explicitly specified, but the review draws from environmental, behavioural, and computer science fields.

findings.antecedent: Effective wayfinding system (correct placement, position, size of signs, maps, other wayfinding aides)
findings.consequent: Flow of people in built environments (e.g., train/bus stations, airports, malls)
findings.quote: if people are able to find their way in a built environment in an efficient manner... then the flow of people... will be such that they will be able to reach their desired destination as quickly as possible

findings.antecedent: Understanding of wayfinding principles and elements
findings.consequent: Design of spaces for efficient and quick wayfinding (e.g., emergency evacuation)
findings.quote: If the principles and elements of wayfinding are understood, then spaces can be designed to ensure that this process can be undertaken as quickly and efficiently as possible.

findings.antecedent: Lack of generic airport terminal design, different locations/operations of critical points (check-in, security, gates)
findings.consequent: Confusion and disorientation in airport terminals
findings.quote: Airport terminals are often characterized by confusion and disorientation

findings.antecedent: Correct placement and accuracy of signs and maps (especially during emergency evacuation)
findings.consequent: Ability of passengers to evacuate terminal quickly
findings.quote: passengers must rely on the correct placement and accuracy of signs and maps in order to be able to evacuate the terminal as quickly as possible.

findings.antecedent: Impairments to mobility, hearing, and vision (disabilities)
findings.consequent: Wayfinding complexity
findings.quote: For those in the population with impairments to their mobility, hearing and vision, wayfinding can become more complicated.

findings.antecedent: Clarity of signage in airports
findings.consequent: Passenger progress and satisfaction
findings.quote: airports can best facilitate passenger progress and improve satisfaction by focussing on key elements, one of which was the clarity of signage.

findings.antecedent: Understanding and correct application of wayfinding principles and elements
findings.consequent: Frustration and customer experience
findings.quote: The understanding and correct application of the principles and elements of wayfinding will help to reduce frustration, leading to improved customer experience.

findings.antecedent: Being lost (poor wayfinding)
findings.consequent: Tangible costs (lost staff time, reduced staff concentration, lost business, missed appointments, delayed meetings, lawsuits, failure to meet targets, injury/death)
findings.quote: the cost associated with being lost is tangible.

findings.antecedent: Well-designed environment
findings.consequent: Comprehension of the environment and ability to find one's way and maintain direction/orientation
findings.quote: A well-designed environment encourages comprehension of the environment and can assist users to find their way and maintain a sense of direction and orientation.

findings.antecedent: Spatial orientation (ability to form a cognitive map)
findings.consequent: Successful wayfinding
findings.quote: Spatial orientation is defined as a person's ability to form a cognitive map

findings.antecedent: Route choice strategies (e.g., least angle, initial segment, least turns, fine-to-course)
findings.consequent: Mental and physical efforts involved in moving through the environment
findings.quote: Route choice is affected by implicit strategies that minimize the mental and physical efforts involved in moving through the environment

findings.antecedent: Language used to communicate directions (e.g., cardinal directions, route instructions, distances, relative frames, landmarks)
findings.consequent: Person's ability to successfully form spatial orientation and undertake successful wayfinding
findings.quote: the language used to communicate directions impacts on a person's ability to successfully form spatial orientation, and hence undertake successful wayfinding.

findings.antecedent: Cultural backgrounds (language differentiation, vocabulary, geographical style, cultural meaning, conversation style)
findings.consequent: Perception of reality, spatial decision-making, wayfinding, cognitive mapping, spatial cognition
findings.quote: Culture also affects the way spatial information is used... Spatial decision-making and wayfinding are impacted by the cultural and social situation of an individual

findings.antecedent: Gender
findings.consequent: Spatial navigation and performance in wayfinding tasks
findings.quote: Differences exist in the spatial navigation skills and spatial abilities of males and females.

findings.antecedent: Testosterone levels
findings.consequent: Performance in spatial and navigational tasks
findings.quote: Testosterone, or the exposure to testosterone, results in increased performance in spatial and navigational tasks.

findings.antecedent: More pronounced right hemisphere on males
findings.consequent: Performance in spatial tasks
findings.quote: More pronounced right hemisphere on males is attributed to better performance in spatial tasks.

findings.antecedent: Lynch's elements of the built environment (paths, edges, districts, nodes, landmarks)
findings.consequent: Organization and navigation of a built environment
findings.quote: Lynch (1960) classified the elements of the built environment as paths, edges, districts, nodes and landmarks.

findings.antecedent: Landmarks (external reference points, e.g., towers, domes, hills, signs, buildings)
findings.consequent: Everyday spatial tasks of wayfinding and navigation
findings.quote: These elements, particularly landmarks, play an important role in the everyday spatial tasks of wayfinding and navigation

findings.antecedent: Maps and signs
findings.consequent: Wayfinding (orientation, direction for decision-making, visualization of connectivity)
findings.quote: Maps and signs are wayfinding devices... that provide information for orientation, direction for decision-making and visualize the connectivity between a current and desired location.

findings.antecedent: Grid configurations of cities/city block matrices
findings.consequent: Comprehension of city layout
findings.quote: Grid configurations of cities or city block matrices are easier to comprehend.

findings.antecedent: Landmarks (salient, contrasting with environment, placed at decision points)
findings.consequent: Wayfinding ease, cognitive wayfinding strategies, orientation
findings.quote: Landmarks make wayfinding easier... The placement of landmarks at decision points affect cognitive wayfinding strategies and facilitate orientation.

findings.antecedent: Cool colors (walls)
findings.consequent: Calming, focus on visual/mental tasks, awareness, direction to destination, perceived navigability
findings.quote: Cool colours are calming and help people focus on visual and mental tasks. Cool colours can increase awareness and help direct people to a destination. It has been shown that cool-coloured walls are seen as more navigable.

findings.antecedent: Warm colors
findings.consequent: Focus outwards, awareness, ease of perceiving space, use as landmarks
findings.quote: Warm colours focus people outwards and increase their awareness. The use of warm colours allows people to more easily perceive the space and it has been shown that warm colours can be effectively used as landmarks for wayfinding purposes.

findings.antecedent: Indoor lighting (low brightness levels)
findings.consequent: Perception of space (negative), emotions, memory, perceptual-orientation, problem-solving abilities
findings.quote: Spaces with low brightness levels are perceived negatively compared to other brightness levels. Increases in the brightness level of a space positively correlated with positive perception of the space.

findings.antecedent: Cool colors and high brightness levels
findings.consequent: Spatially oriented
findings.quote: The use of cool colours and high brightness levels help people to be spatially orientated.

findings.antecedent: Map learning aligned with initial orientation of the map
findings.consequent: Superior performance in spatial tasks
findings.quote: Map learning leads to superior performance only when aligned with the initial orientation of the map.

findings.antecedent: Signage (placed at decision points, direction signage)
findings.consequent: Wayfinding performance, confusion, stress
findings.quote: Signs placed at decision points improve the wayfinding performance. Direction signage has been shown to have the greatest effect on wayfinding... In some settings, signage enhances wayfinding and reduces confusion and stress; however, in other cases, it is ignored or found to be confusing.

findings.antecedent: Textual signage
findings.consequent: Wayfinding errors (wrong turns, backtracks)
findings.quote: Textual signage has been shown to be more effective than graphical signage in reducing wayfinding errors such as wrong turns and backtracks.

findings.antecedent: Graphical signage
findings.consequent: Flow of people in a building
findings.quote: Graphic signage though has been shown to allow for a faster flow of people in a building.

findings.antecedent: Visibility Index (VI) for a terminal (La / N(N-1))
findings.consequent: Ease of wayfinding
findings.quote: By equating ease of wayfinding as a function of the existence of sight lines, the VI is the ratio of the number of sight lines... Higher index values indicate easier wayfinding

findings.antecedent: Inter-connection density (ICD) of a floor plan
findings.consequent: Wayfinding difficulty, accuracy of cognitive map, time to destination, wrong turns, backtracking incidents
findings.quote: Increases in the ICD result in an increase in wayfinding difficulty due to the decrease in the accuracy of the cognitive map formed... It also increases the mean time to find a destination, the average number of wrong terms and the average number of backtracking incidents.

findings.antecedent: Topological complexity of a built environment (measured by ICD)
findings.consequent: Overall legibility of an environment
findings.quote: the topological complexity of a built environment is an important variable that has a large influence on the overall legibility of an environment.

findings.antecedent: Building's spatial configuration (measured by space syntax integration)
findings.consequent: Wayfinding performance
findings.quote: correlations existed between the measures of a building's spatial configuration and indicators of the wayfinding performance.

findings.antecedent: Spatial learning (over time)
findings.consequent: Adaptation to larger organization characteristics of the environment (e.g., space syntax integration)
findings.quote: travel patterns began to correlate strongly with 'integration' and other space syntax global measures which suggests that spatial learning adapts to the larger organization characteristics of the environment.

findings.antecedent: Wayfinding use of axial lines and nodes
findings.consequent: Space syntax integration values
findings.quote: Haq (1999) found the existence of a relationship between the wayfinding use of axial lines and nodes and their space syntax integration values.

synthesis_conclusions: Wayfinding is a complex process influenced by an interplay of human and environmental factors.

Human factors (spatial orientation, cognitive mapping, route strategies, language, culture, gender, biological factors) and environmental factors (paths, nodes, landmarks, districts, maps, signs) are crucial for decision-making and execution in wayfinding.

Motivations for investigating wayfinding include improving people flow, ensuring accessibility for disabled persons, facilitating emergency evacuations, reducing frustration and costs, and enhancing passenger experience, especially in transportation hubs.

Cognitive and mathematical models provide insights into wayfinding, with cognitive models focusing on human aspects and mathematical models (like Visibility Index and Inter-connection Density) quantifying environmental ease of wayfinding.

Space syntax provides tools to analyze spatial configurations and their relationship to wayfinding performance, but has limitations in accounting for individual differences and superficial environmental aspects.
A holistic model that combines both human and environmental elements is vital for a comprehensive understanding of effective wayfinding.
evidence_gaps: A systematic review of wayfinding research has not been undertaken to date.
Cognitively based computation models are based heavily on human aspects of wayfinding and lack environmental aspects.
Mathematical models (VI, ICD) are purely on environmental aspects and do not account for human aspects.
Space syntax ignores some important human and environmental factors (distance, direction, overall shape/layout, individual differences, superficial aspects like colors/patterns/textures).
A holistic model with the ability to include both human and environmental factors and determine their relative importance is currently missing in wayfinding research.
limitations: The review itself is a narrative synthesis and does not employ systematic review methodologies (e.g., formal search strategy, risk of bias assessment).
